tagline: The PDF editor every other one is measured against, plus the compliance output nobody else emits.
verdictSummary: Acrobat is two products on one bill. The first is a toolbox — merge, split, compress, OCR, convert — and open source covers it completely. The second edits the body text of a PDF somebody else authored, with the original fonts and correct reflow, and emits tagged PDF/UA and validated PDF/A. That half is decades of typesetting and standards work, and no personal build gets near it.
coreLoopDIY: Self-host Stirling PDF for the everyday operations, keep every original file untouched, and write each operation to a new versioned output rather than editing in place.
whatYouLose: editing the body text of a PDF you did not author, with fonts and reflow intact
tagged PDF/UA output that passes an accessibility checker
PDF/A archival output that passes a conformance validator
Acrobat Sign and the audit trail behind it
the Microsoft Office, Outlook and browser plug-ins
whyPeopleStillPay: Because in a lot of jobs the deliverable is not "a PDF" but "a PDF that passes the checker" — an accessibility audit, an archival deposit, a regulator's intake form. Acrobat is the tool whose output those checkers were written against.
notes: The toolbox half genuinely is replaceable. It is worth separating the two before deciding you need the subscription.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted PDF workbench for one person.

Deploy Stirling PDF behind a reverse proxy with HTTP basic auth, and put a small wrapper in front of it that does three things Stirling does not: it keeps an immutable copy of every uploaded original in a content-addressed store keyed by SHA-256, it writes each operation to a new file rather than overwriting, and it records an append-only log line per operation with the input hash, the operation and its parameters, the output hash and a timestamp.

Support the operations you actually use: merge, split, reorder, rotate, compress, watermark, redact, OCR with Tesseract, and Office-to-PDF via LibreOffice headless.

Add one conformance step that most tools skip: after any operation, run veraPDF against the output and store the verdict alongside it. When the file is not valid PDF/A or PDF/UA, say so in plain words on the result page. Never label an output "archival" or "accessible" on the strength of having produced it — only on the strength of the validator having passed it.

Out of scope, deliberately: editing existing body text, generating tagged PDF/UA structure, e-signatures, and any cloud account. Editing text inside a PDF someone else laid out is a font-substitution and reflow problem, not a feature you bolt on, and a build that pretends otherwise produces documents that look wrong on somebody else's screen.

Finish by running the operations end to end on a scanned document, a form and a slide deck, and print the log.

faq.q: Can I open my existing Acrobat files in this?
faq.a: Yes — they are ordinary PDFs, and nothing here changes that. What does not travel is anything stored in an Acrobat cloud account: shared review comments, saved Sign templates, and Document Cloud storage links.

faq.q: Will the OCR be as good as Acrobat's?
faq.a: On clean 300 dpi scans of printed text, Tesseract is close enough that you will not notice. On low-contrast phone photos, skewed pages, tables and handwriting it is noticeably worse, and you will end up re-scanning documents you would previously have thrown at Acrobat.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: A small VPS, around $5 a month, or nothing at all if you run it on a machine you already own. Stirling PDF, Tesseract, LibreOffice and veraPDF are all free and everything runs locally — there is no per-document charge.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Compliance output you can defend. If someone requires a tagged, accessible PDF or a PDF/A-2b archive, this build can tell you that your file is not one — but it cannot produce one.
